newsitem.title: USA: Spring flood threat could ebb in U.S. Midwest.
newsitem.headline: Spring flood threat could ebb in U.S. Midwest.

text.p: The partial draining of reservoirs in Montana and the Dakotas plus mild weather across the central United States could diminish the threat of serious flooding in the region this spring, weather experts said on Tuesday.
But the huge amount of snow that fell this winter in the upper Midwest could still trigger flooding in the Mississippi and Missouri River watersheds if there was a rapid spring melt.
"We are not at a state of alarm, but we are being very cautious," said Jack Burns, a National Weather Service hydrologist, when asked about the potential for flooding.
For severe flooding, there would have to be more snow in February and March followed by a rapid melting in April or May, Burns said.

One preventive measure under way was the partial draining of some reservoirs, which would also hold off runoff from spring snow melt. Warmer weather forecast in the area for much of this week should also gradually pare down the snow depths. "Our best scenario is to get high temperatures (soon) and a little bit of rainfall to help melt off that snow cover," Burns said.

Based on current conditions, Burns said there was moderate to high flood potential on the Mississippi River north of Grafton, Illinois, this spring and a moderate potential south of there. He said a high flood potential would mean river levels several feet over flood stage, while moderate potential would be a few feet over.
In 1993, heavy rains flooded both the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers. The Mississippi River at St Louis crested at nearly 20 feet over flood stage.

Joel Burgio, a Weather Services Corp. meteorologist, said warm weather forecast this week for the Dakotas and Minnesota should melt some of the snow. Cooler weather was likely there next week but he did not expect it to produce much snow.
"It appears to be an orderly snow melt, but I can't make any promises at this point," said Burgio.
One development Burgio saw was in the equatorial Pacific, where sea surface temperatures have been warming gradually.
If the warming continued the central United States could have a warm, wet spring "which would be conducive to spring flooding," he said.
